231.t: Told to cut the act to nine minutes, they ran nearly an hour
231.s: Despite the order to do nine minutes, the 14-minute act stopped the show and Paul Ash could not get on.
231.q: We will cut their 14 minutes down to 8 -- down to 9 -- 9 minutes. A 14-minute act, they're going to cut it down to 9 minutes. Now what do we know what to cut out. What do we know what to cut out? We got a 14-minute act, man, that's an act, a perfect act, you know. We don't know what to cut. So I…

231.t: The Ritz Brothers flop at Loew's State and Bubbles' private vow
231.s: After watching the headlining Ritz Brothers die, he vows to quit show business unless Buck and Bubbles headline the next day.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: And we were picked -- the first colored act after Bert Williams. Bert Williams was the first negro that played in the Ziegfeld Follies and Buck and Bubbles was the second negros to play in the Follies. And we -- I took -- that's another job. Billy Rose for the Ziegfeld Follies. How that happened,…

231.t: Seeing Buck and Bubbles on the marquee
231.s: Next morning the marquee has their name in lights; they get a star dressing room with a phone and stop the show.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: : My manager didn't know and my partner didn't know that I had it in my mind not to go on the stage any more and I was going to quit show business if

231.t: Success in the Follies and cutting the act to nine minutes
231.s: They stood out in vagabond clothes and Bubbles' down-to-earth style; he cut the act to nine minutes in rehearsal and still stopped the show when the stage manager threatened to cut the lights.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: We go in this show, man, and never look back. Never look back. It was the greatest show that we ever had in life. Greatest showtime, because we did the shows and the shows were so pleasing that we stood out like a sore thumb, you know. We were the only ones that had vagabond clothes on in the show.…

231.t: Refusing an encore until Harry Richman quieted the house
231.s: He refuses to go back up until Buck presses him; Richman quiets the audience, the stage manager complains, and Nazarro likes it.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: However, when I come down-stairs they're hollering "Buck and Bubbles, Buck and Bubbles." They're hollering "Buck and Bubbles." And up on the stage they're asking if Buck and Bubbles are coming back and Buck is calling me, "Come on, Bubba," I said, "No, forget about it, forget it." And he doesn't…

231.t: Doubling uptown at the Lafayette and downtown at the Follies
231.s: Going from the loud Lafayette to the silent Follies house, with cab-driver trouble, Bubbles tells Harry Leroy he keeps dancing to keep the applause up.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: the ridiculous to the sublime. When we left the Lafayette Theater to go downtown to the Ziegfeld Theater you could hear a pin fall downtown. Uptown, man, you couldn't hear your ears. You didn't know what was happening uptown. Downtown you darsn't spoil a song, it was so quiet, you know.

231.t: The Follies' payoff and tightening the act
231.s: On Tape 6 the Follies made them more marketable; the act stayed the same but tighter.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: That bit would be with E.C. I couldn't think what it would be just to save my soul. That's hard for me to that's hard for me to think of, man. That's so far back. E. C. he come there, that's all I can remember. He come there. No, I can't think of that bit. Don't strike me at all.

231.t: Tightening the act: dancing over the laughs
231.s: Cutting from 14 to 9 minutes meant talking and dancing on top of laughs and applause.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: I've got to tighten up, man. I told you how much time we spent at that hotel getting this act down to

33.t: Floor shows, Dick Shawn, Russ Papalia and Billy DeWolf
33.s: He tells of playing for Dick Shawn and others, using trombonist Russ Papalia as his substitute, and a joke from Billy DeWolf and a critic's review.
33.q: Pat Cooper played bass for him. At the Grand, he plays with the accordionist who also played with me at various times. Of course in my career of over 40 years as a leader I had a lot of different musicians, but always had the best I hope. Some of whom maybe were not considered the best by some…

251.t: Stage acts: Alcorn on the lap and throwing instruments
251.s: Albert and Alcorn did a trick act, fingering each other's horns, and bands generally used showmanship motions.
251.q: Yeah. Well, Alcorn and I had an act together on that. We had this act together. I'd have Alcorn sit on my lap. He was such a young captain. He was small. And we'd blow the horn. I'd cross. I'd blow. I'd finger his horn. He'd finger mine. A little trick that we thought of meant on there. And we'd…

147.t: The band's spontaneous stage show and glee club
147.s: Crawford describes trumpets and trombones thrown and caught, saxophones promenading, and the choral arrangements Sy Oliver began.
147.ch: Precision, the union and learning to read
147.q: Spontaneous, spontaneous. Eddie Durham brought a trick in there, where you throw your trombone and all of a sudden you just let it go, and slide --

232.t: Leon Wright's showmanship, the dress act and Flip Wilson
232.s: Wright steals saxophone battles with Bill Evans and does a dress comedy act with Geesil Minerve that he says Flip Wilson copied.
232.q: But Bill--Yusef, was very clever too and when he learned it, (inaudible). Yusef was a great, big guy and he would be blowing and blowing and Leon would spread his legs out wide and Leon would get off when he started blowing and just go through his legs and when he would do that the house would go…

529.t: Stage show routines and Curtis Porter's back-beat story
529.s: The band turns to showmanship at the Howard Theatre, and Curtis Porter flees a wrong-way back beat at the Glass Bar in St. Louis.
529.ch: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
529.q: Shit, you know. And I got tired of that shit but then the band started going--getting to be a tighter band, you know. 'Cause we started playing in the theatres--the Howard, you know, the Howard Theatres and would--opposite other bands.
